note: Fremont's budget data comes from City documents alone; there is no workbook. Every figure is read from a table row or a sentence quoted from its PDF page (source/excerpts/{source}.json, extracted with pdfjs), and the build parses each number from its quote and ties every table to its own totals. Pages are PDF pages; each source's pageOffset turns them into the printed page numbers receipts cite. fremont.gov refuses automated requests, so the excerpts were extracted from copies downloaded in a browser (Oct 29, 2026); the mid-year report and the proposed-budget presentation are byte-identical to their Internet Archive captures.

notes.caveat: Figures are from the City of Fremont's adopted budget and its budget reports. Years before FY 2026/27 are shown for context and were not adopted with this budget, and years after it are the City's forecast. Not for investment-decision use.

glossary.definition: The adopted budget is the annual City operating budget approved by the City Council for the fiscal year.
An authorization by the City Council to make expenditures and to incur obligations for a specific purpose within a specific time frame.

The budget for a fund is balanced when total budgeted resources, including revenues, transfers in from other funds, and unallocated fund balance from previous years, meet or exceed total budgeted use of resources, including expenditures and transfers out to other funds.
The retirement system, administered by the State of California, to which all regular City employees belong.
The five-year financial plan for improving assets and integrating debt service and capital assets maintenance, adopted in a separate budget document and updated every two years.

Cost centers are funds established to account for the transactions and activities related to specific City services, and the fees are used for the benefit of the fee payers. The Development Cost Center, for example, is a fund that accounts for services related to planning, engineering, and inspection of public and private development construction projects.
Payment of the principal and interest on an obligation resulting from the issuance of bonds, notes, or certificates of participation (COPs).
A twelve-month period of time to which a budget applies. In Fremont, the fiscal year is July 1 through June 30.
An independent fiscal and accounting entity with a self-balancing set of accounts, used to record all financial transactions related to the specific purpose for which the fund was created.
The difference between fund assets and fund liabilities.
The primary fund of the City used to account for all revenues and expenditures of the City not legally restricted as to use. This fund is used to accumulate the cost of the City’s general operations.
A tax imposed on travelers who stay in temporary lodging facilities within the City. Also referred to as a Transient Occupancy Tax.
Facilities on which the continuance and growth of the community depend, such as roads, sidewalks, parks and public buildings.
The Finance Department’s three-year forecast of revenues and expenditures.
Appropriations of the General Fund not directly associated with a specific department. Expenditure items and certain types of anticipated general savings are included.

The proposed budget is the budget that is sent to the City Council by the City Manager. The proposed budget, including changes made by the City Council during its review, is approved and then becomes the adopted budget.
This fund type is used to account for City revenues from sources that, by law or administrative action, are designated to finance particular functions or activities of government.

Amounts transferred between funds; not considered a revenue or expense. For example, legally authorized transfers from a fund receiving revenue to the fund through which the resources are to be expended are shown as operating transfers.
